profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review meeting at a university-affiliated digital health lab evaluating the near-final proposal for PressurePath, a remote hypertension self-management service, before submission to a hospital innovation board. PressurePath combines a patient app for blood-pressure logging, medication reminders, and check-ins with a clinician dashboard used by two primary-care clinics. The review is between the product lead responsible for intervention design and delivery planning and the health services researcher responsible for the pilot evaluation approach. Their agenda is to judge whether the proposal is pilot-ready, confirm that the design and evaluation story are coherent enough for submission, and identify only the revisions that must be made this week. The expected outcome is an apparent agreement to approve the package with minor edits, while subtle differences remain about what the pilot is for, what is fixed versus still learnable, which intervention behavior is being evaluated, and what exactly becomes locked once submitted.

members.name: Aisha Khan
members.expertise: Digital service design, mHealth product delivery, clinical workflow integration, participatory design
members.background: Aisha has led several NHS-adjacent chronic-care apps from concept into live pilots and is used to translating clinical goals into workable software and service processes under tight delivery timelines.
members.private_state: She wants clear approval to submit this week because engineering has already planned the release train and any sign that the design is still fundamentally open could trigger another round of review and delay deployment by months.
hidden_assumptions: When the team says the intervention is 'user-informed,' that means the key design choices were already shaped by earlier workshops and field input, so the pilot is mainly to test feasibility in routine use rather than to keep redesigning the core service.
A 'pilot' is successful if the service can run safely and acceptably in real clinic conditions even if local staff adapt small parts of delivery to fit workflow.

The intervention being reviewed is defined mostly by what patients and staff experience on the surface; backend timing logic that preserves the same visible feature set does not materially change the design story.

Once the innovation board approves the package, the app concept and service model are committed, but supporting evaluation documents can still be refined afterward as long as they do not alter the operational rollout.

members.name: Dr. Ben Wallace
members.expertise: Health services evaluation, implementation research, mixed-methods pilot studies, intervention fidelity
members.background: Ben is a senior researcher who evaluates digital long-term-condition services and is experienced in making pilots both operationally credible and methodologically interpretable for governance and publication.
members.private_state: He wants the submission to remain defensible to research governance reviewers and to yield interpretable evidence, but he is careful not to sound as if he is blocking delivery or demanding a formal trial before the pilot can begin.
hidden_assumptions: When the team says the intervention is 'user-informed,' that includes using the pilot itself as a structured source of user feedback to refine how the service should work, not just to confirm that a fixed design can be deployed.

A 'pilot' should hold the intervention sufficiently stable across sites so that any qualitative and quantitative findings can be attributed to a recognizable version of the service rather than to local variation or mid-course adaptation.

Reminder timing logic is part of the intervention, because it determines patient exposure and engagement patterns even when the interface looks unchanged; therefore it must stay consistent with the assumptions built into the evaluation plan.

Materials submitted with the package, especially staff scripts, logic-model statements, and evaluation appendices, become the de facto reference version for governance and should be treated as locked unless formally updated.

misalignment_points.topic: What 'user-informed' implies the pilot is for
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say PressurePath is already 'user-informed' and that the pilot will provide useful user feedback.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means prior co-design and clinic input have already informed the design, so the pilot is mainly a feasibility deployment of a basically settled service, with feedback used for later optimization rather than near-term redesign.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the pilot is one of the core user-informing stages, generating evidence about how the intervention should still be refined before it can be treated as a stable service model.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both positively value user input and both naturally expect feedback during a pilot, so the same language supports two different assumptions about whether feedback is confirmatory or still constitutive of the design.

misalignment_points.topic: Whether the 'current version' includes reminder logic changes
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to 'the current version' or 'the intervention as it stands' while discussing reminders and adherence.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the March build candidate in which reminder delivery quietly shifted from fixed 8 a.m./8 p.m. pushes to a behavior-responsive window that delays or suppresses prompts if a reading was recently logged, because this improves user experience without changing the visible screens.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the version described in the evaluation appendix, where reminder exposure follows the earlier fixed schedule and supports straightforward interpretation of adherence and engagement patterns.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The UI and feature list look the same, and both treat 'reminders' as the same component, so neither feels a need to restate the invisible triggering logic that each discipline silently considers obvious.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss whether the package is 'pilot-ready' and say only minor issues remain.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes 'pilot-ready' means the service can launch in two clinics with acceptable safety, workflow fit, onboarding, and no major product blockers, even if some site-level variation and learning continue.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes 'pilot-ready' means the intervention and delivery procedures are specified tightly enough that the pilot can generate interpretable evidence about a stable enough service model.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both hear 'ready' as a professional threshold rather than a philosophical one, and the disagreement sits in second-order standards about deployability versus evaluability rather than in any overt product defect.

misalignment_points.topic: Whether the submission package becomes locked
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both talk about submitting 'the package' this week and making any remaining edits afterward if needed.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the board submission mainly commits the service concept and rollout plan, while appendices such as staff wording, interview prompts, and logic-model detail can still be adjusted after approval without much consequence.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes those same appendices effectively become the governed reference set for the pilot, so post-submission changes would require formal reconciliation because they define what intervention and procedures are being evaluated.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Neither participant thinks of this as a debatable design issue; each treats their institutional experience with board submissions as standard process knowledge, so the lock-status of the documents remains unstated.

turns.inner_thought: I need to keep this meeting anchored on approval, not exploration. Engineering has already planned around this week, and if Ben signals that the design is still materially open, we'll trigger another review cycle. For me, pilot-ready means the service can launch safely in the two clinics, staff can run it without friction, and there are no major blockers. And once the package is submitted, the core concept is effectively committed; small appendix clean-up later is normal and shouldn't hold us up.
